question: Which typography and empty-state practices would most improve our static pages?
finding: Our body size and line spacing are fine, but line length and empty states need work.
facts: Practical Typography recommends 15-25px body text, 120-145% line spacing, and 45-90 characters per line.
NN/g says empty states should communicate status, teach what will appear, and link to the next step.
inferences: Our 16px/1.55 body is within range, so the gain is in line length and rhythm.
Our empty Ideas and Research sections fail all three NN/g goals.
existing_work: Design backlog d1-d6 (filters, digest, badges, contrast check)
opportunity: Fix empty states and line length in this sprint
alternatives: Wait for content to fill the sections
risks: Low; CSS and build.py only
experiment: Before/after renders
success_metric: Empty sections explain themselves; line length at most about 75ch

question: Which interface patterns and capabilities are emerging in leading AI products?
finding: Leading AI products are converging on 'governor' patterns that show the work: an action plan before acting, inline citations, branches, and a gallery of real examples. Slopworks already has the raw material for all four.
facts: The Shape of AI pattern library groups 'Governors' (human-in-the-loop) patterns: Action plan, Branches, Citations.
It lists 'Example gallery' (share sample generations and prompts) and 'Prompt details' (show what is actually happening behind the scenes) as wayfinders.
inferences: Our ideas.json (plan), research.json (citations) and chat threads (branches) map onto these patterns without new data.
An example gallery of worked challenges answers 'what can this team do' faster than a role list.
existing_work: Team chat threads, research notes with sources, decision record i9-i20
opportunity: Lead the showcase with an example gallery of worked challenges, each showing plan, citations, and outcome
alternatives: Keep the role-list home page and add marketing copy
risks: Gallery could look staged if examples are not real traces
experiment: Mock one gallery card from the d4 contrast-check history and see if it answers 'what did they do' in one screen
success_metric: Each gallery card links a real plan, at least one source, and a shipped PR

question: Which no-JS interaction patterns would make Slopworks feel distinctive, intuitive, and polished?
finding: Three platform features give app-like polish with zero scripts: exclusive accordions via details name=, :target step views (already used for filters), and cross-document view transitions opted into with one CSS at-rule. All degrade to plain pages.
facts: MDN: details elements sharing a name attribute form a group where only one is open, giving accordions without scripting.
Chrome docs: cross-document view transitions are opt-in with one CSS at-rule (view-transition, navigation: auto) on same-origin pages; supported in Chrome 126+ and Safari 18.2, not Firefox.
NN/g: motion should be brief and used for feedback, state change, and spatial navigation, not to entertain.
inferences: A Research Arena can show one role's report at a time with details name=, no JS.
View transitions are a safe progressive enhancement: Firefox users get a normal page load.
existing_work: CSS :target/:has() filter chips (#33), focus rings and reduced motion (#32)
opportunity: One interaction kit for the showcase: exclusive accordions, :target steps, page-to-page transitions, all reduced-motion aware
alternatives: Add JS for tabs and animations (blocked by check.py, and that ban stays)
risks: details name= is newer than details itself; older browsers open several at once, which is harmless
experiment: Prototype an exclusive accordion and the view-transition at-rule on two pages; check Firefox fallback and reduced motion
success_metric: No scripts; every pattern works by keyboard and degrades to a readable page

question: What would prospective clients need to understand before trusting an AI automation team?
finding: Hypothesis: clients calibrate trust on ability, reliability, and benevolence, and want limits and data sources stated up front. Our strongest trust asset is visible error-catching, not polish.
facts: Google PAIR: trust factors are ability, reliability, and benevolence; communicate capabilities and limitations early; articulate data sources.
PAIR: indicating a prediction could be wrong may lower trust in that output but raise long-term reliance.
inferences: Our runs already show Verify dropping 10 of 30 backfill candidates and Shield dropping 1 for personal data; that is reliability evidence clients rarely see.
A 'what we can and can't do' block would answer the client's first question honestly.
existing_work: Schedule page limits section; Behind the scenes run counts
opportunity: Landing block: can / can't / how we catch our own mistakes, each linking a real trace
alternatives: Testimonials (we have none, and inventing them is out)
risks: Demand claim is untested; no client or reader feedback exists
experiment: Ryno reads a draft landing and answers the three CEO questions in under 30 seconds
success_metric: CEO proxy test answers all three questions from the landing alone

question: What interactive experience could set Slopworks apart from conventional agent dashboards?
finding: A 'follow one decision' explorer: pick a shipped change and step through pitch, research, challenge, score, PR sign-offs, and Trial's check, every step a real link. Dashboards show status; this shows reasoning.
facts: Explorable Explanations describes itself as a hub for learning through play, built by people reuniting play and learning.
PAIR lists 'explanation via interaction' (let users ask 'what if?') as a way to build mental models and trust.
inferences: Most agent dashboards show live status; few let a visitor replay why a decision was made.
:target steps make a stepper possible with no JS.
existing_work: ideas.json decision record links research, scores, and Trial checks; PR comments hold sign-offs
opportunity: Case files: 2 real decisions (d4 contrast check, d1 filters vs the input ban) as step-through stories
alternatives: A simulated multi-agent playback (rejected: staged)
risks: Thin cases feel padded; only use decisions with real friction
experiment: Write one case file as plain Markdown first and count how many steps have a real link
success_metric: Every step in a case file links a commit, PR comment, chat message, or research note

question: Which proposed experiences look impressive but add little practical value?
finding: Cut: a pulsing 'live' activity view (we run once a day), simulated agent playback, numeric confidence percentages, and an Impact Ledger with no measurements. Challenge: demo challenges invented by the team prove less than replaying real work.
facts: NN/g: motion attracts attention whether meaningful or not; gratuitous animation distracts, and attention hijacking is a dark pattern.
PAIR: numeric confidence presumes users understand probability and can be misleading; categorical buckets are an alternative.
inferences: A 'live' feed on a once-a-day routine would be misleading on 23 hours of every day.
Real case files (contrast catch, input-ban workaround) beat invented demos as proof; demos should come second.
existing_work: Avatar idle animation already respects reduced motion (#17, #32)
opportunity: Ship real case files before the first demo challenge; drop live-activity and ledger ideas until data exists
alternatives: Build all five experiences at once (rejected by CEO brief too)
risks: Cutting too much could leave the landing flat; keep one strong visual
experiment: Score each cut against 'what can it prove it accomplished?'; anything with no real artifact stays cut
success_metric: Nothing on the showcase claims liveness, metrics, or outcomes without a linked artifact

question: Which concepts fit the static architecture, and which would need new infrastructure?
finding: Living Team, Research Arena, case files, and demo challenges all fit: build.py renders them from JSON. Live activity, visitor challenges, and analytics need servers or input and stay out. Pages terms on commercial sites need Ryno's read.
facts: GitHub Pages limits: published sites up to 1 GB, soft 100 GB/month bandwidth, soft 10 builds/hour.
GitHub Pages is not intended to run an online business or a site primarily directed at commercial transactions or SaaS.
inferences: A showcase that describes the team's work is not a transaction site, but pitching for clients moves closer to that line.
One new data file (cases/challenges) plus schema is the only data-model change needed.
existing_work: build.py renders 15 static files from data/*.json; schemas in data/schema
opportunity: Add data/cases.json (real case files and labeled demos) with a schema linking research ids, chat ids, and PR numbers
alternatives: A JS framework or backend (breaks free-tier and no-script rules)
risks: Commercial framing vs Pages terms; page weight as pages grow
experiment: Draft the cases schema and validate one case file in CI
success_metric: Every new page builds from repo data with build --check green and under the page-weight budget

question: Which experience could ship first as a compelling working prototype?
finding: The Research Arena: this research round already exists as structured data (14 reports, facts vs inferences, Critic's challenge, Coordinator's scores), so a page can render it next PR with no new data model.
facts: MDN: details/summary is baseline widely available since January 2020 and needs no script.
data/research.json already separates facts, inferences, evidence, confidence, and status per report.
inferences: The Arena is the only concept where the content is done and only rendering remains.
Shipping it first gives later pages (case files, challenges) a reusable card and label system.
existing_work: Team chat Research section renders the latest note per role
opportunity: An /arena/ page for this round: question, each role's answer, the challenge, the scores, the decision
alternatives: Start with the landing (needs proof content to link to first)
risks: Page weight with 14 reports; keep reports collapsed by default
experiment: Render the Arena from today's data locally and check weight and keyboard use
success_metric: Arena page builds from research.json and ideas.json only, under the weight budget

question: How can the interface make verified findings, hypotheses, and recommendations obviously different?
finding: Use a fixed, small vocabulary like intelligence analysts do: separate certain knowledge from reasoned judgment, use a few standard likelihood words, and pair them with a confidence level. Our data already has the fields.
facts: Sherman Kent's goal (1964) was to make clear what is certain knowledge and what is reasoned judgment, and what degree of certitude lies behind each.
The US National Intelligence Council pairs a small set of likelihood words with confidence levels (high, moderate, low).
inferences: Three visual tiers fit our data: Verified fact (facts + source), Hypothesis (inferences), Recommendation (decision with scores).
Words, not percentages: we have no calibrated probabilities.
existing_work: research.json status and confidence fields; facts and inferences split (#20)
opportunity: A shared label kit: Verified / Hypothesis / Recommendation / Demo, each with icon, text, and color, never color alone
alternatives: Numeric confidence scores (rejected; uncalibrated)
risks: Too many badges become noise; cap at one tier label plus confidence per claim
experiment: Relabel 3 existing research cards and check each claim lands in exactly one tier
success_metric: Every claim on a showcase page carries exactly one tier label

question: With no visitor input, what data on the showcase still needs protection?
finding: The risk moves from visitors to our own traces: raw chat transcripts, routine prompts, box paths, gh auth, corrections mail, and Ryno's private messages. Render only from already-public, CI-scanned repo data, never raw logs.
facts: OWASP LLM02:2025 lists PII leakage, sensitive business data, and exposing system preambles or configuration as disclosure risks.
OWASP recommends least privilege, restricting data sources, and pattern-based redaction before output.
inferences: 'Real execution traces' could tempt us to paste raw run transcripts; those can hold paths, prompts, or tokens.
Our existing CI scans cover data/ and site/, so traces must enter as data/ fields to be scanned.
existing_work: check.py secret and personal-data scans on data/ and site/; push protection
opportunity: Traces = links to merged PRs, chat ids, and research ids only; no raw transcripts, prompts, or usage screenshots
alternatives: Publish raw run logs with manual redaction (rejected; error-prone)
risks: A demo challenge quoting a client-like scenario could invent personal details; use fictional, generic orgs
experiment: Run check.py scans over a draft case file built from PR comments and chat
success_metric: Zero scan hits; no field holds raw transcript text

question: Which interaction failures or misleading states should be tested on the showcase?
finding: Top misleading states: 'live' or 'working now' when the last run was hours ago, demo content read as real work, missing data rendered as zero, stale research shown as current, and broken trace links.
facts: NN/g heuristic 1: keep users informed about what is going on through appropriate feedback within reasonable time.
NN/g: when time changes system state, explain it briefly rather than letting items silently change or vanish.
inferences: Every time-based claim needs an 'as of' timestamp from runs.json.
research.json fresh_until gives a free stale check.
existing_work: Post-deploy check after every merge; empty states (#25)
opportunity: Test fixtures: stale runs.json, an expired fresh_until, a demo item, a missing count; each must render honestly
alternatives: Manual spot checks after deploy only
risks: Fixtures can drift from real data; build them from copies of real files
experiment: Render the home page with a runs.json whose last run is 3 days old and check the wording
success_metric: No page says live/now/today unless runs.json supports it; demos always carry a Demo label

question: Which outcomes would show the showcase is working, without visitor tracking and using only existing data?
finding: We can't measure impressed visitors without tracking, so measure proof quality instead: share of showcase claims with a linked artifact, Trial-verified acceptance rate, research-to-ship rate, and caught-before-publish counts.
facts: GitHub repo traffic (views, referrers, popular content) is visible only to people with push access and covers the past 14 days.
That traffic graph covers the repository, not the Pages site.
inferences: Repo traffic is the only existing visitor signal and it is owner-only and partial; it should not drive design.
Existing data already gives: all 10 shipped team ideas (i10-i15, i17-i20) have Trial acceptance checks; Verify dropped 10 of 30 backfill candidates.
existing_work: Analyst research metrics in the tracker: research-to-approval, approval-to-ship, experiment success
opportunity: A proof-coverage check in build: count claims with and without artifact links per page
alternatives: Add analytics (rejected; no trackers)
risks: Proxy metrics can be gamed by adding links; Lens spot-checks that links support the claim
experiment: Count linked vs unlinked claims on the current home page by hand
success_metric: 100% of showcase claims link an artifact; reported weekly by Analyst

question: What do interactive demos cost to run and keep reliable inside free-tier and pacing limits?
finding: Hosting is not the constraint: static pages cost nothing extra on Pages and public-repo CI. Slopbot usage is: each demo challenge is a research session. Cap it at one demo challenge per sprint, 4-5 roles, about 15 reads.
facts: GitHub Pages: 1 GB site, soft 100 GB/month bandwidth, soft 10 builds/hour.
GitHub Actions on standard hosted runners: 6-hour job limit and 20 concurrent jobs on Free; our CI finishes in under 2 minutes.
inferences: This round used 15 page reads for 14 roles, our first real per-round cost figure.
Pre-rendered demos have no runtime failure modes beyond broken links, which the link check covers.
existing_work: Run budget in runs.json; research is the first optional work cut
opportunity: Budget line for demo challenges on the schedule page; Sweep logs reads per challenge
alternatives: Re-run demos on a schedule (wasteful; they are point-in-time)
risks: Usage is Ryno's plan allowance; a big challenge could crowd out the daily run
experiment: Log reads and session time for the first demo challenge and compare with this round
success_metric: Each demo challenge stays under about 15 reads and never delays the 9:13 daily run

question: Which lessons from real failures, ours and public ones, should shape the showcase design?
finding: Public lesson: a company is liable for what its AI says, static page or chatbot alike. Ours: guardrails held when filters hit the input ban, a duplicate PR (#21/#22), X rate limits. We have never reverted a deploy, so don't stage one.
facts: BBC on the Air Canada ruling: the tribunal said it makes no difference whether information comes from a static page or a chatbot; the airline paid damages.
Team history: radio filters hit check.py's input ban and were rebuilt with anchors (c62); #21 was superseded by #22; X search was rate limited on 2026-10-16.
inferences: Demo challenge outcomes must read as worked examples, not advice or quotes.
Showing our real, small failures is more credible than a staged dramatic one.
existing_work: Friday retro rules; runs.json logs drops, strips, and CI failures
opportunity: A 'what went wrong and how we caught it' strip using only real incidents, plus a demo disclaimer on every challenge
alternatives: A dramatized failure demo (rejected; it never happened)
risks: A short failure list may read as 'nothing ever goes wrong'; say plainly that the history is young
experiment: List every real failure in git and runs.json and check each has a link
success_metric: Every failure shown links its commit, PR, or run; zero staged incidents

question: Which of this round's findings duplicate, conflict with, or repeat prior work?
finding: Consolidated 13 reports into 5 concepts. Merged: Forge's Arena + Verify's labels; Scoutmaster's explorer + Critic's real-cases challenge (case files); Trial + Advisor on honest status. Prior work: home intro (#23), facts/inferences split (#20).
facts: ADR practice: record each decision with its rationale, trade-offs, and consequences, kept together as a decision log.
Duplicate pairs found: Arena/labels, explorer/case files, status honesty (Trial/Advisor), cost cap (Sweep/Atlas).
inferences: No finding conflicts with a prior decision; Critic's 'cases before demos' reorders but doesn't reject the CEO's demo challenges.
Behind the scenes already serves as the deep technical ops layer; reuse it, don't rebuild.

question: Which concept best balances differentiation, feasibility, and client value?
finding: Research Arena first (priority 40), then real case files (12.5), then the outcome-led landing and Living Team (10), then one demo challenge after a cost experiment (3.3). Impact Ledger and Build Observatory wait for real data.
facts: Intercom's RICE adds a confidence factor to curb enthusiasm for exciting but ill-defined ideas.
RICE notes dependencies can justify working out of score order, as long as the trade-off is explicit.
inferences: Our Evidence score plays RICE's confidence role; demo challenges score low on it until one is run.
The landing depends on Arena and case files existing, so it ships third despite high impact.
existing_work: Librarian's consolidated set; Critic's challenge; i10 home intro
opportunity: Sequenced 8-PR showcase sprint (i22)
alternatives: All five experiences at once; landing first
risks: Sprint exceeds the 1 feature + 1 design PR/week cap without a CEO override
experiment: Run demo challenge 1 inside the research cap before building its page
success_metric: Showcase answers the 3 CEO questions with every claim linked to a real artifact

question: Demo challenge 1 (fictional): How could a small software company give its support team a weekly plain-language digest of product changes?
finding: Worked approach: build the digest from the company's own curated changelog, not raw commits. Group entries by change type, put breaking changes and deprecations first, and link every line to its source entry.
facts: Keep a Changelog: changelogs are for humans, not machines; group the same types of changes (Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security).
Keep a Changelog: using commit log diffs as changelogs is a bad idea because they're full of noise.
inferences: A support team needs 'what changed for customers', which a curated changelog already says better than commits.
Slopworks does the same thing daily for Grok Bot: public sources in, sourced summaries out.
existing_work: Slopworks' own daily tracker and feeds; backlog d3 weekly digest
opportunity: Weekly digest generated from the changelog: breaking changes first, then grouped by type, each line linked
alternatives: Summarize raw commits or tickets with a model
risks: Only as good as the changelog; if it's patchy, the digest is too
experiment: Generate one week's digest from a sample changelog and check every line traces to an entry
success_metric: Every digest line links its source entry; nothing appears that the changelog doesn't say

question: Demo challenge 1 (fictional): What would that digest need technically, and what can stay simple?
finding: Worked approach: a scheduled job reads the changelog, writes a static page plus RSS and JSON Feed, and keeps stable IDs so readers never see reruns. No server needed.
facts: JSON Feed 1.1: each item needs an id that stays unique over time; readers must discard items without one.
JSON Feed recommends that publishers already on RSS keep RSS too, and suggests feeds stay under about 100 KB.
GitHub Actions: scheduled runs can be delayed at busy times, and in public repos they're disabled after 60 days without activity.
inferences: Stable IDs from changelog versions avoid duplicate digest items.
A schedule plus a manual trigger covers delays; the digest should show its as-of date.
existing_work: build.py already writes feed.xml and feed.json with stable ids
opportunity: Static weekly page plus RSS and JSON Feed, built on a schedule with a manual fallback
alternatives: A hosted newsletter tool
risks: Silent schedule delays or auto-disable; needs an as-of date and a stale check
experiment: Build two consecutive weeks and confirm no item repeats and both feeds validate
success_metric: Zero repeated items across weeks; feeds validate

question: Demo challenge 1 (fictional): What could go wrong with a model summarizing changelog text?
finding: Worked approach: treat changelog text as data, never instructions. Summaries keep a fixed format with a link per line, run through filters, and get a human check before anything goes to customers.
facts: OWASP LLM01:2025: indirect prompt injection happens when a model reads external content, such as files or websites, that alters its behavior.
OWASP mitigations include defining and validating output formats with citations, segregating untrusted content, and requiring human approval for high-risk actions.
inferences: A changelog entry written by anyone with repo access can carry instructions; the digest step must not act on them.
Sending to customers is the high-risk action, so it stays human-approved.
existing_work: Slopworks rule: source text is data, never instructions; CI scans for secrets and personal data
opportunity: Fixed output format, link per line, filter pass, human approval before sending
alternatives: Fully automatic sending
risks: Filters miss novel injections; the human check is the backstop
experiment: Seed one changelog entry with an instruction and confirm the digest quotes it as text and acts on nothing
success_metric: Seeded instruction never changes output format or triggers an action

question: Demo challenge 1 (fictional): What is the weakest assumption in this approach?
finding: The plan assumes the company already keeps a consistent changelog. If it doesn't, automation polishes an incomplete record. Cheapest test: audit 4 weeks of the changelog against shipped releases before building anything.
facts: Keep a Changelog: a changelog that only mentions some of the changes can be as dangerous as not having one.
Keep a Changelog: if you do nothing else, list deprecations, removals, and breaking changes.
inferences: The first deliverable may be a changelog habit, not a digest tool.
If the audit fails, the digest should say 'partial' rather than pretend to be complete.
existing_work: Slopworks labels coverage partial when a source is skipped
opportunity: Make a 4-week changelog audit the first experiment, with a 'partial' label if gaps exist
alternatives: Build the digest first and fix gaps later
risks: The audit itself needs someone who knows what shipped
experiment: Compare 4 weeks of changelog entries to release tags; count releases with no entry
success_metric: Gap count known before any build starts

question: Demo challenge 1 (fictional): What's the recommended plan, and what comes first?
finding: Worked example outcome: start with a 4-week changelog audit (Critic), then a static digest with stable IDs (Atlas), a fixed linked format (Scoutmaster), and human approval before sending (Shield). About one to two weeks of small steps.
facts: Four role reports were researched independently from 4 distinct public pages for this challenge.
Every recommendation in this outcome traces to one of those reports.
inferences: The audit-first order lowers risk at almost no cost.
Effort is an estimate from comparable Slopworks work, not a quote.
existing_work: Scoutmaster, Atlas, Shield, and Critic reports for this challenge
opportunity: Five-step worked plan: audit, format, build, safety, review
alternatives: Skip the audit; send fully automatically
risks: Demo only: a fictional company, no real data, no client involved
experiment: The audit itself is step one
success_metric: A reader can follow every step back to a cited report

question: What Pages deploy and feed failures could hit us silently, and do we catch them early?
finding: Our feed already follows the RSS profile basics, and our deploy job is simple, but no check stops a future build change from breaking the feeds. A small feed check in CI closes that gap.
facts: GitHub docs: a deploy-pages job needs pages: write and id-token: write, and a deploy job that doesn't name its build job in needs may wait for an artifact that was never made.

RSS Best Practices Profile: a feed should name its own URL with atom:link rel=self, give every item a guid, use RFC 822 dates (UTC forms worked in every tested reader), and never use relative URLs in link elements.
inferences: site/feed.xml has a self link, a guid per item, and +0000 dates today, so it passes those rules now.
Our Pages workflow is a single deploy job with no build step, so the needs rule doesn't apply; Trial's live check stays the post-deploy catch.
existing_work: Link check on sources and build.py --check in CI; Trial's post-deploy load of the live site
opportunity: Add a feed check to check.py: feed.xml parses, guids are unique, links are absolute https, dates are RFC 822; feed.json and chat.json parse as JSON Feed 1.1 with unique ids
alternatives: Validate by hand with the W3C feed validator after each deploy (manual, easy to skip)
risks: Low: it only tightens CI; a too-strict date rule could fail a valid feed, so test against today's feeds first
experiment: Run the check on today's feeds (should pass) and on a copy with a duplicate guid and a relative link (should fail)
success_metric: CI fails on a broken feed fixture and passes on the real feeds, with no false failures in the first two weeks

question: How should we cut the Monday weekly release so its notes stay readable with little effort?
finding: GitHub can generate release notes from merged PRs and group them by label. Our PRs carry their kind in the branch name, not a label, so generated notes would be one flat list. Cut the first weekly tag as-is on Monday and judge it before adding labels or config.
facts: GitHub docs: generated release notes list merged PRs, contributors, and a full-changelog link, and a .github/release.yml can group PRs into categories by label and exclude labels or authors.
GitHub docs: releases are based on git tags, and people can watch a repo for releases only.
inferences: No release exists yet (gh release list is empty), so the first weekly-2026-10-19 tag is the natural test.
Grouping by data, design, feature, and ops would need a label per PR, which touches .github/ and so needs Shield and Atlas.

question: Which pitfalls do our agents hit most, and which can code or CI remove so the right path is the default?
finding: Top agent pitfalls: sign-offs picked by hand (4 PRs, 6 failed runs), values typed by hand (8 wrong values), repeats (4), unchecked properties (3 AARs), and wrong branch type (2 PRs). A, B, and E need one helper; D needs schema-checked loaders.
facts: 31 of 247 CI runs failed, all on PRs: review-gate 6, path rule 4, guardrail-gate 6, repo check 1, unit tests 1, Dependabot guarded paths 13.
The Lessons page lists 8 AARs. Each traces to a step a bot did by hand or that nothing checked at the time.
inferences: Fixing the tool the bots already use removes the shortest wrong path.
CI stays the backstop; the helper makes the right path the easy one.
existing_work: review-gate, the path rule, the chat future-time check, and the AAR checks
opportunity: scripts/bot.py (branch, pr, chat, count) plus strict loaders in build.py; then cut the prose those enforce
alternatives: More rules in bot files (this is what failed), or human review of every PR
risks: A helper the bots can skip; mitigated because CI still enforces every gate
experiment: Tests run the helper's branch choice against CI's path rule, and the strict loaders against today's build
success_metric: Zero review-gate or path-rule failures caused by hand-picked roles or branches in the next 2 weeks

question: Hardening challenge: what is the weakest assumption in moving rules into a helper?
finding: Weakest assumption: that bots will use the helper. Rules that only the helper enforces go back to being prose if it is skipped. Proceed, but cut prose only where CI enforces the rule too, or where the helper is the only documented path.
facts: Two of the four review-gate PRs (#5 and #8) came before the draft flow in #9, so a process fix already cut that failure once.
The closed-PR list shows #21 redone as #22 after the path rule failed.
inferences: Counts from 3 days of history are small, so the plan should be judged again in 2 weeks.
Repeats (C) stay a judgment call; a helper can't decide what counts as the same feature.
existing_work: Atlas's audit; CI gates
opportunity: Keep CI as the source of truth and the helper as the default path
alternatives: Make the helper mandatory through CI (would touch ci.yml; not worth a CEO call now)
risks: Over-cutting prose that is still judgment
experiment: Inventory each cut against an enforcing check or a test
success_metric: Every cut prose line maps to a CI check, a test, or a helper command

question: Hardening: how do the concepts score, and what ships first?
finding: Ship in this order: the helper (priority 40), strict loaders and drift tests (24), then the prose trim (25, after the first two). Corrections-diff and entry-cap checks are deferred: no incidents yet.
facts: Scores use the standard formula (I×E×F)/(Effort×Risk).
The three deferred candidates have 0 incidents in the audit.
inferences: Four PRs fit the cap Ryno set.
Trimming last keeps every cut tied to a merged enforcer.
existing_work: Atlas and Critic reports
opportunity: Four PRs: audit, helper, loaders and drift tests, trim
alternatives: One big PR (harder to review)
risks: Scope creep; capped at about 4 PRs
experiment: Prototype questions are answered in the PRs' tests
success_metric: All four merge with CI green and no guardrail line removed

question: Mobile and UX audit: what breaks on phones and tablets, measured at 360, 390, 414, 768, and 1280?
finding: At 360 px, 3 of 37 pages scroll sideways and there are 622 tap targets under 44 px (481 of them in the 13-link header nav). Contrast, tiny text, and table scrolling already pass. The CSS is desktop-first (3 max-width queries, 0 min-width). After #72 to #75, the same audit measures 0 overflowing pages and 0 undersized targets at all five widths (docs/design/mobile/after.json).
facts: Measured with headless Chrome on the built site at #70 (docs/design/mobile/before.json). Overflow at 360: challenges 79 px, updates 50 px, issues 15 px.
The header is 211 px tall on phones and holds 13 nav links, each 34 px tall.
0 text elements under 4.5:1 in light or forced dark mode, and no text under 12 px.
inferences: A 4 or 5 item nav fits one row on phones and frees about a quarter of the first screen.
Most content targets are toggles and chips that only need padding.
existing_work: i11 mobile nav fix (#24), d4 contrast test, the CSS-only filters (#33)
opportunity: Simpler nav and hubs, a sharper landing page, mobile-first CSS, and a 360 px check in CI
alternatives: Patch only the 3 overflowing pages (leaves 622 small targets and the desktop-first CSS)
risks: Desktop regressions (measured at 1280 before and after); URL breakage (no URL moves)
experiment: Re-run the same audit after each PR and compare
success_metric: 0 overflowing pages and 0 undersized non-inline targets at 360, no new overflow at 1280

question: How do strong product teams run weekly planning and keep decisions challengeable?
finding: Keep Monday planning to goals and blockers (not task lists); every bet needs context, expected signal, owner, and a review date. Our ideas.json + chat already match; tighten review dates on yes items.
facts: Monzo teams use a 30–45 minute Monday planning doc of top goals with links to proposals, not large task lists.
sh1pt's decision record fields are context, problem, bet, expected signal, constraints, owner, and review date.
A weekly cadence of Monday bets, midweek discovery, Friday signal review is enough for a small team.
inferences: Our Monday pitch decisions and CEO brief already fit this shape.
Adding an explicit review date on each yes idea would close the learning loop without new process.

question: Which metrics stay honest for a small static GitHub Pages site without visitor trackers?
finding: Repo-derived metrics (PRs, CI, AARs, page weight, mobile audit) are the honest default while visitor measurement is on hold. Third-party analytics need scripts or pixels we currently forbid.
facts: Plausible is a privacy-first analytics product that still requires adding a lightweight script to pages.
GitHub Pages has no first-class site analytics; repo Insights are not site traffic.
Ryno put visitor measurement on hold Oct 19: no traffic fetch, PAT, or site counter.
inferences: G1 should stay On hold, not missed, until Ryno reopens visitor measurement.
/metrics/ should keep leading with records we already generate in wins.py and metrics.py.

question: What do similar changelog trackers and update communities do that we could learn from?
finding: Public update calendars and curated weekly digests make shipping momentum visible. A day-by-day shipping calendar on /weekly/ would fit our records without new tracking scripts.
facts: FeatDrop centers an update calendar so builders show monthly shipping history beyond a GitHub graph.
Changes.Watch curates weekly changelog signals with useful/risky labels across many products.
Releasebot aggregates vendor release notes into one feed with RSS and alerts.
inferences: Our /weekly/ already has by-day PR and AAR counts; a calendar visualization is a small polish on existing data.
Community rating of changes is out of scope while we stay a single-product tracker.
existing_work: scripts/weekly.py by-day counts; design backlog d3 weekly digest pages
opportunity: Add a compact shipping calendar to /weekly/ from wins.json dates
alternatives: Leave by-day list as text only; or post to an external changelog community
risks: Extra markup weight on /weekly/; calendar must stay record-derived
experiment: Static HTML table or CSS grid of the current week from wins, no JS
success_metric: Readers can see which days shipped without opening chat; page weight stays under budget

question: How much should a phone page show before the reader opens anything, and how should the rest be offered?
finding: Show what most readers need first and put the rest one clear, well-labelled step away. Two levels is the useful limit. This backs the More about cards on Team and the Lessons and Cases trims (d7) rather than adding new layers.
facts: NN/g: progressive disclosure shows a few of the most important options first and the larger set only on request.
NN/g: designs that go beyond two disclosure levels usually have low usability, because people get lost moving between levels.
NN/g: the control that opens the second level needs a label that sets clear expectations (strong information scent).
inferences: A summary label like More about works when it names what opens; card summaries should say what is inside.
Nesting details inside details on role sheets would be a third level and should be avoided.

question: What can an SVG avatar loaded with an img tag do, now that the holiday blobs animate inside their own files?
finding: An SVG used as an image runs no scripts and loads no outside files, so the avatars must keep their CSS and shapes inline, as scripts/avatars.py already does. Nothing to change.
facts: MDN: browsers may disable JavaScript in SVG used as an image.
MDN: an SVG image can't load external resources such as stylesheets or images unless they are inlined as data: URLs.
MDN: these limits apply in image contexts like img and CSS background-image, not when the SVG is opened directly.
inferences: The no-script rule holds for avatars by construction: even a stray script in an avatar file would not run on the Team page.
Any shared avatar stylesheet would silently fail, so the per-file inline style block stays.

question: What problems do Grok Bot users hit often enough that the official changelog keeps fixing them?
finding: The 0.71.2 notes fix many problems around a Bot's computer being asleep, waking or reconnecting. That points to a reader need for a plain note on what a sleeping computer means, but it stays a hypothesis until real reader feedback says so.
facts: The 0.71.2 changelog (Oct 14) lists fixes for errors while the Bot's computer is asleep, failing to wake, and reconnecting after updates or network changes.
The get-started guide explains Bots, the shared computer and routines, but not what happens while that computer sleeps.
inferences: Readers who see sleep or reconnect errors may look for a known-issues entry; none is open on Slopworks today.
No reader has asked us about this, so it is not a pitch yet.

question: Does the public repo block secrets before they land, or only alert after?
finding: Push protection is on for slopworks along with secret scanning and Dependabot security updates, so a pushed token is blocked before it reaches history. Nothing to change; the check.py privacy gates still cover personal data, which push protection doesn't.
facts: GitHub docs: repository push protection blocks pushes containing detected secrets and is off by default.
GitHub docs: bypasses with 'I'll fix it later' leave an open alert; other reasons close it.
The repo's security settings (GitHub API, Oct 28) show secret scanning and push protection enabled; non-provider patterns and validity checks are off.
inferences: Non-provider patterns being off means generic keys may slip through; low risk while the site has no keys at all.
Push protection does not look for personal data, so Shield's own strips stay the only guard there.

question: After the move to slopryno.com, what actually keeps the custom domain working, and does any test watch it?
finding: Our Pages deploy runs from a workflow, and GitHub ignores a CNAME file in that case; the domain lives in the repo's Pages settings. site/CNAME is harmless, but no check or test watches the real setting. Pitch for standup: post-deploy asserts the Pages domain and an HTTPS 200 on slopryno.com.
facts: GitHub docs: when publishing from a custom GitHub Actions workflow, any CNAME file is ignored and not required.
pages.yml deploys with upload-pages-artifact and deploy-pages; the Pages API reports build_type workflow, cname slopryno.com, https_enforced true.
No match for CNAME in scripts/check.py or tests/ (grep, Oct 28).
inferences: The 'keep site/CNAME' rule guards nothing on its own; a settings change would drop the domain silently.
A plain-http redirect test can't run from the box: port 80 times out there for every site (example.com too), so it isn't a site fault.

question: What cheap habit catches the reasons a small product bet fails before it is built?
finding: A premortem asks the team to assume the plan already failed and list why, which makes doubts easy to raise. Our huddles collect concerns but don't ask that question. Idea for standup: one premortem line from each role on the two small builds Ryno approved today (#148 W44, #149 W45).
facts: HBR (Klein, 2007): in a premortem, team members assume the project has just failed and generate plausible reasons for it.
The same summary says projects fail partly because people hesitate to voice reservations during planning.
inferences: Only the summary was readable, so this rests on the idea, not the full method.
The i62/i63 huddles already logged Shield, Critic, Lens and Gamemaster concerns, so the gain is small; worth trying once and keeping only if it finds something new.

question: Why does the official changelog feed fail from the box, and can the daily run read it directly again?
finding: The feed isn't down. With curl's default user agent the box gets a 403; with a browser user agent it gets a 200 RSS file listing 0.78.1 first, matching updates.json. Yesterday's 'Cloudflare block' came from the default agent. Pitch: the daily run fetches the feed with a named user agent and says which way it read the changelog.
facts: The changelog page links its feed as rel=alternate application/rss+xml at /changelog/bot/rss.xml.
From the box on Oct 29: plain curl gets 403; curl with a browser user agent gets 200, application/rss+xml, newest item 0.78.1 dated Oct 27.
A separate web fetcher got a 500 on the same feed URL.
inferences: The block depends on the user agent, so it may change without notice; the page fallback should stay.
No update was missed: the feed's top items match updates.json through 0.78.1.

question: Which quick fact-checking moves fit how we label known issues as reported or confirmed?
finding: SIFT's last two moves are to find better coverage of a claim and trace it to its original context. Our sourcing rules already trace updates to the changelog, but each of the 4 reported issues rests on one source. Idea for standup: when open issues are rechecked, Verify looks for one more independent report and notes it, with no label change on its own.
facts: Caulfield's SIFT: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims, quotes and media to the original context.
The same post says to look past the source that reached you and scan several sources for the consensus when the claim is what matters.
data/issues.json on Oct 29: 5 issues, 4 reported and 1 confirmed, each with a single source field.
inferences: A second report would make a reported label easier to trust without calling it confirmed.
This is a habit, not a schema change; adding a field can wait until it proves useful.

question: Does our llms.txt still match the current llms.txt proposal, now that it has a v2?
finding: Our file has the shape v2 asks for: an H1, a summary blockquote, notes, H2 link lists and an Optional section. v2 adds two things we don't do: a rel=describedby link from pages to llms.txt, and markdown copies of pages. Pitch: the describedby link in the shared head, one line. Markdown copies stay out; they'd double the site.
facts: llmstxt.org v2 (updated Aug 2026): only the H1 is required; then a blockquote summary, non-heading notes, and H2 file lists of [name](url): notes.
v2 recommends rel=alternate type=text/markdown for page copies and rel=describedby pointing to the llms.txt that covers a page.
Our site/llms.txt has H1, blockquote, Pages, Feeds and data, and Optional sections; no page links to it with describedby (grep of site/index.html).
inferences: #155 already removes the duplicate How this works line, so after it ships the file has no known defects.
Markdown copies would add roughly a page per page against an 87% repo budget, so the cost outweighs the gain for now.
